title: Adani and Abu Dhabi Are Building a $11.5 Billion Aluminium Complex in Odisha. It Would Be India's Biggest Foreign Metals Investment Ever.
excerpt: The 50:50 joint venture with the UAE's IHC will produce 2 million metric tons of aluminium a year, create 53,500 jobs, and raise India's smelting capacity by half. The announcement comes as a US judge keeps Adani's criminal case alive.
body:
Adani Group and Abu Dhabi's International Holding Company have signed a deal to build India's largest aluminium complex in Odisha, a $11.5 billion joint venture that will mark the single biggest foreign investment in the country's metals sector.

The memorandum of understanding, signed on July 2 with the Odisha state government, lays out a 50:50 partnership between Adani Enterprises and IHC's subsidiary International Resources Holding. The project would raise India's total aluminium smelting capacity by nearly 50 percent — a bet that the metal's role in everything from electric vehicles to data centres to renewable energy infrastructure will only grow.

## The Scope of the Complex

The numbers are massive. The integrated facility will include a 4-million-metric-ton-per-year alumina refinery, a 2-million-metric-ton aluminium smelter, a 4,000 MW captive power plant, and a 1-million-metric-ton downstream manufacturing park. Odisha Chief Minister Mohan Charan Majhi called it the state's largest FDI proposal ever.

The project is expected to create 53,500 jobs — 35,000 during construction and 18,500 once operations begin. That is roughly the workforce of a mid-sized Indian city materializing around a single industrial complex.

Odisha was the natural choice. The eastern state sits atop some of India's richest bauxite reserves and already accounts for 54 percent of the country's aluminium output. Adani Ports' Dhamra facility on the Bay of Bengal coast provides ready logistics infrastructure. The state government, under Majhi's BJP administration, has been aggressively courting industrial investment since coming to power in 2024.

## Adani's Metals Expansion



> **""Rising demand from digitisation and manufacturing is driving the group's long-term strategy," he said."**


This is Adani Group's second major metals venture, following the copper smelter in Gujarat's Mundra that began operations last year. The aluminium play signals a broader strategy by Gautam Adani to diversify the conglomerate beyond its traditional strengths in ports, energy, and infrastructure.

The timing is deliberate. Global aluminium demand is being reshaped by three converging forces: the energy transition (solar panel frames, wind turbine components, EV bodies), the data centre boom (server chassis, cooling systems), and India's own infrastructure push. India currently imports significant quantities of value-added aluminium products — this complex would allow domestic production to substitute for those imports.

Karan Adani, who is increasingly taking on strategic roles within the group, appeared at the MoU signing to explain the rationale. "Rising demand from digitisation and manufacturing is driving the group's long-term strategy," he said.


![Abu Dhabi — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9c/Abu_dhabi_skylines_2014.jpg/3840px-Abu_dhabi_skylines_2014.jpg)


## The Gulf Connection

The IHC partnership underscores the deepening economic ties between India and the Gulf states. IHC, controlled by Sheikh Tahnoun bin Zayed Al Nahyan, Abu Dhabi's national security adviser and one of the UAE's most influential royals, has been building its India portfolio systematically. The company previously increased its stake in Adani Enterprises to over 5 percent and co-founded Sirius Digitech, a joint venture focused on AI and digital transformation.

The $11.5 billion investment comes on a spectrum of Gulf capital flowing into India. Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund, Qatar Investment Authority, and Abu Dhabi Investment Authority have all expanded their Indian portfolios in recent years. For the UAE specifically, India has become its largest non-oil trade partner, and the IHC-Adani aluminium venture deepens the relationship from financial investment into industrial partnership.

## The Shadow of the Courthouse

The announcement arrives against a complicated backdrop. On June 26, a U.S. federal judge in Brooklyn declined to immediately dismiss criminal charges against Gautam Adani stemming from an alleged bribery scheme related to solar energy projects in India. Judge Nicholas Garaufis ordered the Justice Department to justify its May decision to drop the prosecution, calling the government's explanation "terse, bland and conclusory." The DOJ has until July 13 to respond.

Adani Group has consistently denied wrongdoing. The company settled a related civil case with the SEC, with Gautam Adani paying $6 million and nephew Sagar Adani paying $12 million, without admitting fault. A separate OFAC settlement over alleged Iran sanctions violations cost the group $275 million.

The Adani Group's stock market performance suggests investors are looking past the legal cloud. Adani Enterprises shares surged to near their 52-week high following the Odisha announcement and a simultaneous qualified institutional placement, returning over 40 percent year-to-date — dramatically outperforming the Nifty 50's 6.9 percent decline.

## What It Means for Odisha

For Odisha, the deal is transformational on paper. The state has long been mineral-rich but industrially underdeveloped, exporting raw bauxite and iron ore while the value addition happened elsewhere — often in Gujarat. Majhi emphasized that his government is committed to "leveraging its mineral wealth to spur manufacturing and prosperity" rather than simply extracting and shipping raw materials.

The project's downstream manufacturing park is the critical piece. If it materializes as planned, Odisha would not just mine bauxite and refine alumina — it would produce finished aluminium products for the automobile, construction, and electronics industries. That is where the employment and the margins are.

The timeline for completion has not been disclosed. Mega-projects of this scale in India typically take five to seven years from MoU to first production, and not all survive the journey. But the combination of Adani's execution track record in ports and energy, IHC's deep pockets, Odisha's resource base, and favourable state government policy makes this more credible than most.

India currently produces about 4 million metric tons of aluminium annually. If this complex reaches full capacity, it would add 2 million metric tons — a 50 percent increase that would reshape the country's position in global metals markets.
